paper_metadata.title: Exceptional High-Temperature Strength and Creep Properties of a Weldable Ni-Based Wrought Superalloy

evidence.quote: Herein, the tensile and creep properties of a weldable Ni-based wrought superalloy specifically engineered to endure service temperatures surpassing 800 °C have been investigated.

The chemical composition of the interest alloy is listed in Table 1. The as-cast cylindrical ingot of the alloy was prepared using investment casting at the Beijing Institute of Aeronautical Materials.

The rods underwent a solid solution treatment at 1160 °C for 4 h, subsequently subjected to a two-step aging process comprising an initial aging at 1080 °C for 4 h, followed by a secondary aging at 845 °C for 20 h.

The purity of the raw metals used for melting alloys was set to be higher than 99.9%. The vacuum degree inside the vacuum induction melting furnace shall be no more than 2 Pa; after the master alloy ingot is melted, the refining temperature is controlled at 1530–1550 °C

the pouring temperature is set to 1390–1410 °C, and the mold shell temperature is maintained at 930 °C, with a pouring rate of 0.9–1.1 kg s/C0 1 and a total pouring weight of 8 kg. Upon completion of pouring, the power supply shall be turned off, and a holding time of no less than 5 min is required.
The as-cast ingot was then solution-treated at 1120 °C and 1170 °C for 1 h, respectively, and hot-forged longitudinally into rods with a diameter of 40 mm.

The a/2 <110> matrix dislocations traverse the γ matrix, encountering γ' precipitates, where they are unable to penetrate but instead loop around them, conforming to the Orowan bypass mechanism.

Upon encountering a γ' particle, a pair of a/2 <101> matrix dislocations dissociates, with one partial dislocation entering the γ' precipitate to create an SISF and the other, an a/6 <121> partial dislocation, residing at the γ/γ' interface.

As shown in Figure 8, dislocations exhibit a curved configuration around γ' phases, forming distinct dislocation loops. This observation confirms that the primary deformation mechanism under 800 °C/280 MPa and 870 °C/200 MPa is Orowan looping.
